title: How to Choose the Customer Value That Sizes Your CX Problems
summary: Use the customer value finance already publishes: ARPU for subscription, ACV for B2B, annual spend for retail, net revenue for marketplaces.
body_markdown:
A theme is growing. It drags on[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) . Then someone in the leadership meeting asks what it's worth. To answer, you need a dollar value per customer. Most[customer experience (CX)](https://getthematic.com/insights/customer-experience-statistics) teams reach for[lifetime value (LTV)](https://getthematic.com/insights/motivate-stakeholders-voc-customer-lifetime-value/) , then find they don't have a clean per-customer figure anyone trusts.


The short answer: use the customer value your finance team already publishes, matched to your business model. For subscription businesses, that's average revenue per user (ARPU) or annual revenue per customer. For B2B contracts, it's annual contract value (ACV), averaged by segment. For retail, it's annual spend per customer, built from average basket value and purchase frequency. For marketplaces, it's net revenue per user, never gross transaction volume. Use segment averages rather than individual values. Then write the assumption down in one sentence before anyone sees the number.


Thematic's[Revenue at Risk score](https://getthematic.com/product/revenue-at-risk) is built around this choice. It accepts lifetime value, ARPU, annual contract value, or average basket value, set as one figure or per segment. Below are six steps to pick a basis finance will sign off on, plus a worked example and the mistakes that sink the number.


## The six-step process


1. **Start with a number finance already publishes.** Borrowed credibility beats a better metric nobody recognizes.
2. **Match the value basis to your business model.** Subscription, B2B contract, retail, and marketplace each have a natural unit.
3. **Use segment averages, not individual values.** Two segments beat thousands of contract values.
4. **Match the value to the horizon of the risk.** Annual value for annual decisions. Lifetime value only when finance models it.
5. **Write the assumption in one sentence.** State the basis, the source, the segments, and what it excludes.
6. **Get sign-off before the meeting.** A pre-agreed number survives challenge.


## Step 1: Start with a number finance already publishes


The best customer value is rarely the most accurate one. It's the one your CFO has already seen in a board pack. If finance reports ARPU monthly, use ARPU. If sales reports annual contract value by tier, use that.


Bring a new metric and the debate turns to your metric. Bring finance's own number and the only open question is the churn assumption.


The common mistake is building a bespoke LTV model in a spreadsheet. Lifetime value is, by definition,[an estimation and prediction of the net profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_lifetime_value) a customer contributes over the entire future relationship. It rests on retention, margin, and discount-rate assumptions. Each one is a new place for a skeptic to push.


## Step 2: Which customer value fits your business model?


Pick the unit that matches how revenue is actually earned.


**Business model** **Value basis to use** **Why** **Watch out for**


Subscription (B2C or self-serve SaaS) ARPU or annual revenue per customer Revenue is recurring and fairly even per customer An LTV that bakes in the churn rate your CX fix is meant to change


B2B contract Annual contract value, averaged per segment Finance already reports it by tier Pulling named contract values into a feedback tool


Retail or transactional Annual spend per customer (average basket value × purchase frequency) Captures repeat purchase, not one trip A single basket value, which undersizes loyal customers


Marketplace Net revenue per user (your take), per side Gross volume isn't your revenue Gross merchandise volume (GMV), which overstates exposure


Annual contract value is[subscription revenue per contracted customer, normalized across a year](https://www.paddle.com/resources/acv-vs-arr) . That makes it comparable across multi-year deals. For marketplaces,[GMV doesn't equal revenue](https://a16z.com/13-metrics-for-marketplace-companies/) . Revenue is the portion of GMV the marketplace keeps. Sizing a CX problem on GMV can inflate the figure several times over, and finance will spot it.


If your marketplace has two sides (buyers and sellers, riders and drivers), value each side separately. A seller leaving often takes many buyers' transactions with them, so the per-user values rarely match.


## Step 3: Why segment averages beat individual customer values


Segment averages beat individual customer values for sizing CX problems. There are three reasons.


- **Averages are defensible.** A segment average comes from a finance report. An individual figure comes from a customer relationship management (CRM) record that may be out of date.
- **Averages match the question.** A CX theme affects a group of customers. You're sizing a problem, not predicting which account churns.
- **Averages keep sensitive data out of the feedback tool.** Exact contract values are commercially sensitive, and feedback analysis doesn't need them. The[data minimization principle](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/data-protection-principles/a-guide-to-the-data-protection-principles/data-minimisation/) in UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 5(1)(c) says personal data should be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary." A segment average is usually all that's necessary.


Start with the split finance already uses, such as Enterprise and small business, or loyalty members and everyone else. Two segments plus a default is enough for most rankings. More segments add precision you probably can't defend.


Thematic's[Revenue at Risk](https://help.getthematic.com/article/227-revenue-at-risk) works this way. An admin sets one value for everyone, or splits the base into segments with different values. A Default segment catches everyone else, so incomplete data never blocks the figure. No CRM integration and no contract data are required.


## Step 4: Match the value to the horizon of the risk


Pick a value that matches the time frame of the decision. If leadership is setting this year's roadmap, use an annual value (ARPU × 12, ACV, or annual spend). It answers one question: what do we stand to lose over the next year?


Use lifetime value only when finance already models it and agrees on the horizon. Standard LTV models typically look three to seven years ahead, and anything further is treated as too speculative. A CX figure built on a seven-year LTV looks large. It's also the first thing a CFO discounts.


A useful rule: if you can't say which year the revenue would be lost in, the horizon is too long.


## Step 5: Write the assumption in one sentence


The assumption statement keeps the number alive after the meeting. Put it directly under the figure on every slide. Include four things:


1. **The basis.** ARPU, ACV, annual spend, or net revenue per user.
2. **The source and date.** Which report, which quarter.
3. **The segmentation.** How many segments, and what the default covers.
4. **What it excludes.** Margin, acquisition cost, referral value.


A template you can copy:


"Revenue at risk uses FY26 Q2 annual contract value from the finance revenue report, averaged across two segments (Enterprise and Mid-market), with a default value for all other customers. It's gross annual revenue, not margin, and excludes referral and expansion value."


Stating the exclusions does two jobs. It heads off the obvious challenge. It also signals the real exposure is probably larger, which is the conservative position a CFO trusts.


## Step 6: Get sign-off before the meeting


Send the assumption statement and segment values to your finance partner a few days ahead. Ask one question: "Would you defend these numbers if someone challenged them?" If yes, you can say finance agreed the inputs.


In Thematic, an admin sets up Revenue at Risk once per lens, from Manage Lenses > Configure Lens > Scores. Every analyst who opens the score sees the same customer values. An info tooltip shows the full chain: sample size, what it scaled to, every condition in force, the formula, and the total. When finance asks how the number was built, the answer is on screen.


## A worked example


Take an illustrative B2B software company. Finance reports average ACV of $40,000 for Enterprise and $6,000 for Mid-market. There's no reliable per-account LTV.


- **Basis:** ACV, because finance reports it quarterly.
- **Segments:** Enterprise at $40,000, with a default of $6,000 for everyone else.
- **Horizon:** one year, because the fix competes for this year's roadmap.
- **Assumption:** written with the template above and confirmed by the finance partner.


In Thematic, the admin enters the total customer base and these values, then defines at-risk conditions, each with a[churn likelihood](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-perform-churn-analysis) . Revenue at Risk multiplies each at-risk respondent's segment value by that likelihood and scales the result to the full customer base. Themes re-rank by the revenue behind them. The team[presents the top three themes in dollars](https://getthematic.com/insights/build-business-case-cx-initiative) , with the assumption line under the chart.


The team presents it as an indicative estimate: a defensible ranking of what to fix first, not a forecast.


[Connecting feedback to dollars](https://getthematic.com/insights/roi-of-cx/) pays off. A top-10 grocery retailer reported $4.8M in projected annual revenue from a single six-month pilot, from product-selection opportunities Thematic surfaced. A[Forrester Total Economic Impact study](https://getthematic.com/forrester-total-economic-impact-study) of Thematic found a 543% three-year ROI, with payback in under six months.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Using GMV in a marketplace.** Use net revenue per user, because GMV isn't what you earn.
- **Defaulting to lifetime value because it sounds strategic.** Use an annual figure unless finance already models LTV.
- **Importing individual contract values.** Use segment averages, which are easier to defend and keep sensitive data out.
- **Using a single basket value in retail.** Multiply by purchase frequency so loyal customers aren't undersized.
- **Mixing value bases in one figure.** Pick one basis per analysis so the total adds up.
- **Showing the number without the assumption.** Put the one-sentence statement under every chart.


Picking the value basis is the smallest part of[sizing a CX problem](https://getthematic.com/insights/revenue-at-risk-customer-feedback) . It's also the part most likely to get the number thrown out. Borrow finance's figure, average it by segment, and state it plainly. Then the conversation moves to what matters: which problem to fix first.
